findings.title: Do not pipe unverified remote install script into sh in Dockerfile
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` downloads and runs whatever the URL serves at build time, as root, with no pinned version, checksum or signature. Anyone who controls or compromises that host, or the network path, can run arbitrary code in the build and put it in the shipped image. That is a supply-chain hole, and it also makes builds non-reproducible because the script can change between builds. `-s` hides curl errors, there is no `-f`, and the pipeline has no `pipefail` (alpine's /bin/sh is busybox ash, which has none by default). If curl fails with a DNS error, a 404 or a network failure, `sh` reads empty input and exits 0. The layer then builds successfully without the intended install, which is a swallowed failure.

findings.title: Do not pipe unverified remote script into sh during build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` runs whatever the server returns at build time, as root, in the image. There is no version pin, checksum, or signature check. If the host or the connection is compromised, or the content simply changes, arbitrary code runs in the build and ends up in the shipped image. Builds are also not reproducible. The command is not safe on failure either. `-s` hides errors and `-f` is missing, so an HTTP 404 or 500 body is executed as a script. In Alpine's `/bin/sh` (ash) a pipeline's exit status is the last command's. If curl fails and `sh` receives empty input, `sh` exits 0 and the layer succeeds with nothing installed. `example.com` is also a placeholder domain that does not serve a real installer.

findings.title: Do not pipe unpinned remote script into sh during image build
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` downloads and runs, as root, whatever the URL serves at build time. There is no checksum, signature or version pin, so every build can run different code. A compromised or changed host or redirect (`-L`) gets arbitrary code execution in the image and build environment. The build is not reproducible. The pipe also hides failures. There is no `-f` and no `pipefail`, because the Dockerfile uses the default `/bin/sh -c` shell. If curl fails (DNS error, 404/500 with an HTML body, or empty output), `sh` runs the error body or nothing, and the exit status is that of `sh`. The step can succeed having installed nothing, or run a garbage error page. `-s` also suppresses curl's error output, so the failure is invisible in build logs.

findings.title: Run returns before results are sent; unbounded goroutines ignore ctx
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Run was synchronous: when it returned, every `j*2` had been sent. Now it spawns one goroutine per job and returns immediately, so nothing tells the caller when the sends are done. The usual pattern `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` now closes the channel while goroutines are still sending. That panics with 'send on closed channel', or it silently drops results. If `results` is unbuffered or never drained, each goroutine blocks forever and leaks, because `ctx` is never consulted, so cancellation cannot stop them. The change also spawns one goroutine per job with no bound, and result order is no longer the job order. Run is exported, so this is a public contract change. No in-repo caller exists, so the effect on callers is inferred, not observed.

findings.title: Run returns before results are sent; goroutines unbounded and ignore ctx
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Run sent every result in order and returned only after the last send. Now (src/worker.go:7-9) Run spawns one goroutine per job and returns immediately. A caller that closes `results` after Run returns will make the still-pending goroutines panic with 'send on closed channel'. A caller that stops reading, or that cancels ctx, leaves every goroutine blocked on `results <- ...` forever, because ctx is never checked. Result order is no longer the job order, and the number of goroutines is unbounded (len(jobs)). There is no sync.WaitGroup, no select on ctx.Done(), and no other way for callers to know when the work is finished.

findings.title: Run returns before results are sent; goroutines unbounded and unjoined
findings.whyItBreaks: Before the change, Run returned only after every `j*2` had been sent, in input order. The caller could safely `close(results)` or stop reading as soon as Run returned. Now Run returns immediately after spawning len(jobs) goroutines and nothing waits for them. (1) The standard `Run(...); close(results)` pattern panics with 'send on closed channel'. (2) A caller that treats Run's return as 'done' loses results. (3) Result order is now nondeterministic. (4) ctx is never checked, so if the receiver stops reading, every goroutine blocks forever on `results <-`, a leak proportional to len(jobs). (5) The number of goroutines is unbounded. Run is exported, so the changed behaviour is part of its public contract. No in-repo caller exists, so this was verified by reading the function only.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord uses || and bypasses admin and tenant checks
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version required both `session.isAdmin` and a tenant match. With `||`, the function returns true when the session is admin, even for another tenant's record. That is a cross-tenant delete. It also returns true for any non-admin whose tenantId equals the record's tenantId, so the admin requirement is gone. Both outcomes are privilege escalation. For example, a non-admin in tenant A gets true for a tenant A record, and an admin in tenant A gets true for a tenant B record. No intent to loosen the rule is visible in the diff, and the function takes no other input that could compensate.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord uses || and bypasses admin and tenant checks
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code required both `isAdmin` and a tenant match. With `||`, a non-admin session passes whenever `session.tenantId === record.tenantId`, so any ordinary user can delete any record in their tenant. An admin session passes for any record, so an admin from tenant A can delete tenant B's records. That breaks both the admin-only rule and tenant isolation. Example: `{isAdmin:false, tenantId:'t1'}` with a record `{tenantId:'t1'}` now returns true. `{isAdmin:true, tenantId:'t1'}` with a record `{tenantId:'t2'}` also returns true.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord grants delete to any admin or any same-tenant user
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code required both `session.isAdmin` and a matching tenant. With `||`, either condition alone returns true. A non-admin user in the same tenant can now delete any record in that tenant, which is a privilege escalation. An admin from tenant A can also delete records in tenant B, which is a cross-tenant isolation break. Substitution: isAdmin=false with a tenant match gives true (was false). isAdmin=true with a tenant mismatch gives true (was false).

findings.title: parseSettings swallows parse errors and updateFontSize overwrites settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch-all returns `{...DEFAULTS}` for malformed JSON, a missing or wrong-typed theme, and a missing or wrong-typed fontSize. Before this change, each of these threw. `parseSettings` is exported, so every caller is forced to treat a failed parse as a real value. `updateFontSize` (src/settings.ts:19-23) is the in-repo caller that is affected. If `raw` is corrupt or partial, such as `{"theme":"dark"}` or truncated JSON, it now parses to the defaults, sets fontSize, and calls `save(JSON.stringify(settings))`. That silently replaces the user's stored settings, including their theme, with `theme: "light"`. Previously the error propagated and `save` was never called, so nothing was written.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows all errors and returns defaults, enabling silent data overwrite

Before this change those cases threw and nothing was saved. `updateFontSize` (src/settings.ts:19-22) now treats the fallback as real data. If `raw` is corrupt, truncated, or only partly valid (for example `{"theme":"dark"}` with no fontSize), it sets fontSize on the defaults and calls `save(JSON.stringify(settings))`. That overwrites the user's stored settings, such as theme 'dark', with the default theme. Callers cannot tell a failed parse from legitimately default settings. The catch also hides the intentional `throw new Error("bad theme")` and `throw new Error("bad fontSize")` checks, so they now have no effect.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows errors; updateFontSize persists defaults over user settings

Before this change those cases threw, and updateFontSize aborted without calling save. Now updateFontSize (line 20) gets a valid-looking Settings object, sets fontSize, and calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)) at line 22. Example: raw='{"theme":"dark"}' has no fontSize, so it used to throw 'bad fontSize'. It now saves {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}, which silently resets the user's theme to light. Truncated or corrupt raw input gets overwritten the same way, which loses data. parseSettings is exported, so every caller also loses the ability to tell a failed parse from real defaults.

Saving a draft is legitimately allowed without payment, and a draft is normally unpaid. The payment requirement belongs only to submit, but the shared predicate applies it to both actions.

Now `"draft" !== "ready" && "missing" === "paid"` is false, so saveDraft returns "blocked". Drafts are normally unpaid, so saving a draft is blocked in the common case.

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positivity but accepts negatives and swallows errors
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff renames `read_int` to the public `parse_positive_int`, which newly promises a validated positive integer. The body is unchanged: `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)` (src/parse.rs:2). It does not check the sign, so `"-5"` parses to -5 and `charge("-5")` returns -500, a negative charge. Parse failures (`"abc"`, `""`, overflow) become 0, which is also not positive, and a caller cannot tell them from a real zero. `charge` (src/parse.rs:5-8) is public and now calls the renamed function at src/parse.rs:6. It multiplies the result by 100 with no sign or zero check of its own, so callers trusting the name receive a negative or silent-zero amount.

findings.title: parse_positive_int does not enforce positivity; negatives reach charge()

Very large inputs can also overflow `n * 100`, which panics in debug builds and wraps in release builds.

findings.title: dbg!(items) moves the Vec, breaking the build

The next line, `items.len()`, then fails with rustc E0382 (borrow of moved value: `items`). Even if it compiled, `dbg!` writes to stderr in release builds too, so it is leftover debug output in a production path.

findings.title: changedPaths computed against `latest` but labelled with pinned fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset contract (src/changeset.ts:7-8) says changedPaths were computed against fromRevision and that consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly that revision. The diff changes line 18 to call `readChangedPaths(latest)`, while line 17 still returns `fromRevision: from`, the pinned revision. When `latest` differs from the pinned tag, changedPaths is relative to the wrong base. Replaying it on the pinned revision then silently drops or misapplies changes. The new `latest` resolve at line 15 is used only for this call.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths from pinned revision, not "latest"
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset doc (src/changeset.ts:7-8) says changedPaths are computed against fromRevision and consumers replay them on top of exactly that revision. The diff leaves fromRevision as the pinned tag's revision but calls store.readChangedPaths(latest). Store.readChangedPaths(fromRevision) takes the base revision, so the paths now describe changes since "latest", not since the pinned revision. When latest is ahead of the pinned tag, the result is empty or missing every change between the pinned revision and latest. A consumer replaying onto fromRevision silently drops those changes. No error is raised, so the wrong changeset looks valid. The extra store.resolve("latest") call serves no other purpose.

findings.title: changedPaths computed from `latest` but fromRevision reports pinned revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset interface (src/changeset.ts:7-9) says fromRevision is the revision the changed paths were computed against, and that consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly that revision. After this change, fromRevision is still `store.resolve(pinnedTag)` (line 14, returned at line 17), but changedPaths comes from `store.readChangedPaths(latest)` (line 18). The returned changeset therefore pairs the pinned revision with paths computed relative to `latest`. Whenever `latest` differs from the pinned tag, the paths are the changes since `latest`, not since the pinned revision. A consumer replaying on the pinned revision will silently skip the changes between the pin and latest. The diff gives no reason for using `latest`, and it looks like the wrong variable was passed.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenantId, leaking settings across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey(name) returns `settings:${name}`, and settingsFor (line 12) now uses it instead of `${tenantId}:${name}`. The cache is a module-level Map. After tenant A calls settingsFor('A','theme'), the value is stored under `settings:theme`. A later settingsFor('B','theme') hits the cache at line 13-14 and returns A's value without calling store.fetch for B. This leaks data between tenants and returns wrong settings. invalidate(name) also loses its tenant parameter. It now evicts the entry for every tenant, and the public signature changed from (tenantId, name) to (name). Any caller still passing (tenantId, name) will pass tenantId as the name. That deletes the wrong key and leaves the stale entry in place. The repo has no other callers, so any external caller breaks silently.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenantId, leaking settings across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: cacheKey(name) returns `settings:${name}` with no tenant component, and settingsFor uses it at line 12. The first tenant to request a setting populates the cache. Every other tenant requesting the same name then gets that value from the cache at lines 13-14, and store.fetch(tenantId, name) is never called for them. Example: tenant A calls settingsFor('A','theme') and gets 'dark'. Tenant B then calls settingsFor('B','theme') and gets A's 'dark'. This is a cross-tenant data leak and returns wrong per-tenant configuration. The invalidate(name) signature change at lines 20-21 compounds it. A caller can no longer invalidate one tenant's entry, and any call deletes the shared entry for all tenants.

findings.title: Serialize reserve() so concurrent calls cannot oversell stock
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() reads `remaining` at line 15 and checks it at line 16. It then awaits `store.save` at line 17 and only updates the in-memory map at line 18. The old code did the check and decrement synchronously, so it was atomic. Now the map is not decremented until the await resumes. With stock=1, two concurrent `reserve('a')` calls both read remaining=1 and both pass the `<= 0` check. Both then save 0 and both return true, so one unit is sold twice. With stock=5, two concurrent calls both persist 4 and the map ends at 4, so one reservation is lost.

findings.title: Serialize reserve: stale read across await oversells stock
findings.whyItBreaks: `reserve` reads `remaining` at line 15, then yields at `await this.store.save(...)` on line 17, and only afterwards writes `remaining - 1` at line 18. The check at line 16 and the write at line 18 are no longer atomic. Substituting stock=1 with two concurrent `reserve('a')` calls: both read 1, both pass the `<= 0` guard, both await save, and both return true. One unit is sold twice. Substituting stock=5 with two concurrent calls: both persist and set 4 instead of 3, so a decrement is lost, and the in-memory map and the store both under-count reservations. The previous synchronous version could not interleave this way. Making the method async introduced the race.

findings.title: Fix race in async reserve that oversells and loses decrements
findings.whyItBreaks: `reserve` reads `remaining` at line 15 and checks it at line 16. It then yields at `await this.store.save(...)` on line 17, and only writes the in-memory map at line 18. Before the change the method was synchronous, so the read, check and write could not interleave. Now two concurrent `reserve('a')` calls both read the same `remaining` before either reaches line 18. With stock=1, both pass the `<= 0` check, both save 0, and both return true, so one unit is sold twice. With stock=5, both save 4 and set 4, so one decrement is lost and the persisted and in-memory counts are wrong. Any server-side caller that handles parallel requests (for example `Promise.all` or concurrent handlers) hits this.

findings.title: Update retry.ts for backoff() now returning milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() changed its unit from seconds to milliseconds (`Math.min(30_000, 2 ** attempt * 1000)`). Only the poll.ts caller was updated. src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still calls `sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`, which now multiplies milliseconds by 1000 again. Attempt 0 sleeps 1,000,000 ms (about 16.7 min) instead of 1 s. At the cap it sleeps 30,000,000 ms (about 8.3 h) instead of 30 s. Every failed job attempt therefore stalls for minutes to hours, so retry() effectively hangs.

It can now return nil when the file was not durably written, and callers cannot tell that apart from a successful save. That can cause silent data loss.

The new `defer f.Close()` discards that error, and the function now ends with `return w.Flush()`. On a successful Flush, a Close error is lost and Save returns nil. Close on a written file can report deferred write failures (NFS, quota, full disk), so Save can report success for data that was not durably written. Save is exported, so external callers are forced to treat a failed close as a successful save.

findings.title: Propagate f.Close() error from Save instead of discarding it

Save then returns nil even though the data may not have been fully persisted. Callers cannot tell a failed save from a successful one. Save is exported, so this weakens the public error contract even though nothing in the repo calls it yet.

findings.title: page_window drops the last row of every page (off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) interval (lib/pagination.py:17-21), but the loop at lib/pagination.py:28 uses range(start, end - 1). That excludes the final row of each page. Example: rows=[a,b,c,d], page_index=0, page_size=2 gives start=0, end=2, so the loop reads only rows[0] and returns [a], not [a,b]. A page of size 1 returns nothing. render_page (lib/pagination.py:40) builds on page_window, so rendered output silently omits rows. summarize (lib/pagination.py:52) calls render_page, so it skips one row per page. The original code used range(start, end).

findings.title: TTL comparison inverted: fresh entries miss, expired entries hit
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition changed from `< ttlMs` to `> ttlMs`. A fresh entry (age < ttl) now fails the check, so it is deleted and `get` returns null. That makes every cache read right after `set` a miss and destroys the entry. An expired entry (age > ttl) is returned as valid. The cache therefore serves only stale data and never serves fresh data.

findings.title: pruneDone mutates input while iterating and skips adjacent done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code returned a new filtered array. The new code calls `splice` inside `forEach` on the same array. After each removal the following elements shift left, but the iteration index still advances, so the element right after a removed one is never visited. For `[{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}]`, index 0 is removed, the second done job shifts to index 0 and is skipped, and the result still contains a done job. The function also now mutates the caller's array. The caller's array was previously left intact, so any caller that relied on that breaks.

findings.title: Fix inverted TTL comparison in TtlCache.get
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition is now `Date.now() - storedAt > ttlMs`, which is true only when the entry is expired. Expired entries are returned as hits. Fresh entries fall through to `entries.delete(key)` and return null. A value just set is therefore deleted on its first get and reads as a miss, while stale values are served. The cache is effectively inverted.

findings.title: pruneDone mutates input and skips elements while splicing in forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: The function used to return a new filtered array. It now calls `splice` on the caller's array during `forEach`. Removing an element shifts later elements left, so the next element is skipped. For [{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}], the second done job is never examined and stays in the result. The caller's array is also mutated in place, which breaks any caller that relied on the non-mutating filter behavior and silently loses data from the original list.

findings.title: TTL comparison inverted: fresh entries evicted, expired entries served
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition changed from `< ttlMs` to `> ttlMs`. A fresh entry (age < ttl) now falls through to `entries.delete(key)` and returns null, so every get right after set is a miss and the entry is deleted. An entry older than the TTL is returned as a hit and never evicted. The cache therefore serves stale data indefinitely, and only entries that were never read inside their TTL window can ever be hit.

findings.title: pruneDone splices during forEach, skipping jobs and mutating the input
findings.whyItBreaks: Calling `splice` on the array while `forEach` iterates it shifts the remaining elements left, and the iterator then skips the element after each removed one. For `[{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}]`, index 0 is removed, the array becomes `[done, notDone]`, and iteration moves to index 1 (the not-done job), so the second done job stays in the result. Consecutive done jobs are therefore not pruned. The function also now mutates the caller's array in place, where the previous `filter` returned a new array and left the input untouched. Callers that hold the original list will see it change.

findings.title: Numeric sort replaced by default lexicographic sort
findings.whyItBreaks: `scores.sort()` without a comparator orders elements by their string form, so 100 sorts before 9 and -5 sorts oddly. After `reverse()` the array is not in descending numeric order, so `scores[Math.min(n, len) - 1]` is not the nth-highest score. Example: scores [5,10,100,9], n=2. The default sort gives [10,100,5,9] and the reverse gives [9,5,100,10]. The cutoff is then scores[1]=5, the filter keeps all four players, and `slice(0,2)` returns the players with 5 and 10 instead of 100 and 10. The base code used `(a, b) => b - a`, which was correct, so this is a regression for any scores with differing digit counts or negative values. The consumer is in the same file at src/leaderboard.ts:15, and formatBoard (src/leaderboard.ts:20) also receives the wrong result.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores sort
findings.whyItBreaks: `scores.sort()` with no comparator orders numbers by their string form (UTF-16 code units), not by value. Negative numbers and numbers with different digit counts end up misordered. Example: scores [10, 9, 100] sort to [10, 100, 9] and reverse to [9, 100, 10]. For n=1 the cutoff is scores[0] = 9, so the filter keeps every player (all have score >= 9). `slice(0, 1)` then returns the first player in input order, the one with score 10, not the one with 100. The old code used `(a, b) => b - a`, which was correct. `formatBoard` (src/leaderboard.ts:20) calls `topPlayers`, so the printed leaderboard is wrong too.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores sort
findings.whyItBreaks: `scores.sort()` with no comparator compares elements as strings, so the order is lexicographic. For scores [9, 10, 100] it gives [10, 100, 9], and `reverse()` turns that into [9, 100, 10]. With n=1, topPlayers reads `scores[0]` as the cutoff (src/leaderboard.ts:15), which is 9 instead of 100. The filter then keeps every player, and `slice(0, 1)` returns the first player in input order, the score-9 player, instead of the top scorer. Mixed digit counts and negative scores are also mis-ranked. findings.title: Use constant-time comparison for webhook HMAC signature

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so unmapped changed files are still deep-reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed tail-coverage block was the only guarantee that every changed file is deep-reviewed. Hotspots come from the LLM map pass and are cut by `.slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (MAX_HOTSPOTS=6, line 26). Any changed file that the map omits, or that sits only in a hotspot ranked below the cutoff, is now never deep-reviewed. Nothing in `checked` or `residual_risks` records the gap, so a large PR can return PASS with unreviewed files. The base version of this file had the backstop and said 'never silently skip a changed file'. This is a regression on exactly the large-PR path, where coverage gaps are most likely.

findings.title: Stop discarding deep-pass residual risks in the large-PR merge
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass returns `res.residual_risks`, including blocks=true items the reviewer could not resolve. The change no longer collects them and hard-codes `residual_risks: []` in `candidateMerged`. The critic therefore never sees them, and `deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks)` (line 122) only sees whatever the critic re-invents. An unresolved blocking gap should prevent PASS, but it now silently becomes a clean verdict. The same edit also removed the per-hotspot try/catch that recorded a blocking residual risk when a deep pass failed. That case now throws and aborts the whole review, discarding the other hotspots' results. Failure is no longer degraded into a blocking residual risk, and any non-throwing gap is lost.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so unmapped changed files are still reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: The tail-coverage hotspot was removed. Only the top MAX_HOTSPOTS (6) hotspots from the map pass are deep-reviewed. Any changed file the map pass did not assign to a hotspot, or whose hotspot was cut by `.slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)`, is never reviewed. The map prompt also never sees the diff text. Nothing records these files as unreviewed, no residual risk is emitted, and `deriveVerdict` can return PASS. The removed code's own comment said "never silently skip a changed file". Large PRs with more than 6 surfaces will now ship unreviewed files with a clean verdict.

findings.title: Preserve deep-pass residual risks instead of discarding them
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass returns `res.residual_risks`, including `blocks:true` entries for unresolved gaps. These are no longer collected, and `candidateMerged.residual_risks` is hard-coded to `[]`. The critic and `deriveVerdict` therefore never see them. A deep pass that could not verify something material now yields no blocking signal, and the verdict can be PASS. The previous code accumulated them in `residuals` and passed them to the critic.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual_risks are discarded, so blocking risks never reach the verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass returns `res.residual_risks`. Before this change they were collected into `residuals` and passed to the critic as `residual_risks`. Now the loop at 103-105 reads only `res.findings` and `res.summary`, and `candidateMerged.residual_risks` is hard-coded to `[]` at line 113. Any `blocks:true` risk a deep pass raised (an unverified sentinel, an untraced guard, an unresolved trigger) is lost. The critic receives none of it. The verdict at line 122 is derived only from `pruned.residual_risks`, which the critic produces from the empty candidate. A hotspot whose reviewer said it could not reach a verdict can therefore end as PASS. The failure signal is silently turned into an empty list.

findings.title: Removing the coverage backstop leaves changed files silently unreviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: The large-PR path reviews only `sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (6 hotspots), and only the files those hotspots list. The deleted tail-coverage hotspot was the only thing deep-reviewing changed files that the map pass did not assign to a surface or that were cut off by the slice. Large PRs (over 10 files or over 30k chars) are exactly where this happens. Those files are now never examined, and nothing is recorded in `checked` or `residual_risks`, so the result can be PASS with no sign that coverage was partial.

findings.title: Large-PR review silently drops user focus/deep settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes `focus` and `deep` from `mapBundle` (lines 83-89) and drops the `{{FOCUS}}` substitution from the deep prompt (lines 117-121). In the base version, `bundle.focus` reached both the map pass and every per-hotspot deep pass, and `bundle.deep` reached the map pass. A user who sets a focus or deep mode on a large PR now gets a review that ignores it, with no error or warning. `reviewSmall` still serializes the whole bundle, `focus` and `deep` included, into review.md (line 52-55). The same input now behaves differently depending only on PR size. If prompts/deep.md still contains `{{FOCUS}}`, the literal placeholder text is also sent to the model. The prompts directory is not in this repo snapshot, so I could not check that.

findings.title: Large-PR review silently drops focus/deep options
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code passed `focus` and `deep` into the map bundle and substituted `{{FOCUS}}` in deep.md. The diff removes all three (src/core/review.ts:86-90 and :120). `reviewSmall` still sends the whole bundle, so focus and deep take effect on small PRs only. On large PRs (patch over 30000 chars or more than 10 files) the same flags are ignored with no warning, so large PRs get a different review from the one requested. If deep.md still contains a `{{FOCUS}}` placeholder (prompt files are not in this repo, so this is unverified), the literal token would also go to the model unreplaced.

findings.title: Large-PR review silently ignores focus and deep options
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, `reviewLarge` passed `focus` and `deep` to the map pass through `mapBundle`. It also substituted `{{FOCUS}}` with `bundle.focus` in every deep-pass prompt. Now neither prompt receives them. `reviewSmall` (src/core/review.ts:52-55) still serializes the whole bundle, including `focus` and `deep`, into review.md. So the same flags take effect on small PRs and are silently discarded on large ones. Nothing reports the dropped option to the caller. The `Bundle` still carries the fields, so the options are accepted but have no effect on this path.

findings.title: formatDuration emits '60s' / 'Xm 60s' near minute boundaries
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are floored from raw ms, but seconds are rounded separately from the remainder. When ms % 60000 >= 59500 the rounded seconds equal 60 and no carry goes into minutes. 119600ms gives minutes=1 and seconds=60, so it renders '1m 60s'; the old code rounded to 120s first and rendered '2m 0s'. 59600ms gives '60s'; the old code rendered '1m 0s'. The output feeds the per-step and total durations in the rendered markdown (render.ts:75, :80).

findings.title: formatDuration can emit "60s" / "Xm 60s" after rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code floors the minutes from raw ms, then rounds the remainder separately with `Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000)`. When the remainder is 59500..59999 ms, the rounded seconds equal 60 and the minute is never carried. ms=59600 gives minutes=0, seconds=60, so the output is `60s` (it should be `1m 0s`). ms=119600 gives `1m 60s` (it should be `2m 0s`). The old code rounded to total seconds first and then split into minutes and seconds, so seconds stayed in 0..59. The output is rendered at src/shared/render.ts:75 (per-stage durations) and src/shared/render.ts:80 (total duration).

findings.title: formatDuration can emit '60s' after rounding seconds
findings.whyItBreaks: The change floors minutes from the raw ms value and only then rounds the remainder to seconds. Any remainder in [59500, 60000) ms rounds to 60 without carrying into minutes. ms=119600 gives minutes=1 and seconds=round(59.6)=60, so the output is '1m 60s'. The old code rounded to total seconds first (120s) and printed '2m 0s'. ms=59600 gives '60s' where the old code gave '1m 0s'. This affects the per-step and total durations rendered at render.ts:75 and render.ts:80.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 and empty/blank input
findings.whyItBreaks: The function is exported as `parsePositiveInteger` and throws "requires a positive integer". Changing `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` lets 0 through. `Number("")` and `Number("   ")` both evaluate to 0, so an empty or blank flag or env value now parses silently as 0 where it used to throw. Any caller that treats the result as a timeout, retry count, or limit gets 0 instead of an error. The error message still says "positive", so the new behavior contradicts the function's name and error text. The bug is fully visible in the single changed line, src/shared/runner.ts:32.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 and empty/blank strings
findings.whyItBreaks: The function is exported and named parsePositiveInteger, and it throws "requires a positive integer". The guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so 0 is now returned instead of rejected. Number("") and Number("   ") both evaluate to 0, which is an integer, so blank input that used to be rejected is now returned as 0. The body no longer implements what the name and error message promise. Any caller, including external users of this exported function, that relies on it to reject 0 or blank input loses that check.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 and empty/blank input
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function is named parsePositiveInteger and throws "requires a positive integer", but the guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so 0 now passes. Number("") and Number("   ") also evaluate to 0, so empty or blank values, which were rejected before, are now returned as the valid number 0. Callers that pass the result as a timeout, count, or retry limit get 0, which can mean no timeout or no attempts. That is a silent change from a validation error to a degenerate value. The promise in the name and error message does not match the body.
